qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living in Unit 8: Becoming Independent.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:

**PERSPECTIVES ON BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
In recent years, developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of teenagers and university freshmen recognise the importance of independent life skills, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**managed**</u> these practices into their daily routines at school and in daily life. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to develop essential life skills for independence.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how independent life skills can build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should develop essential life skills for independence, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role at school and in daily life. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living matters for the long-term future. Young people who see teenagers and university freshmen model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, independent life skills not only manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders today but also build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**MAKING BECOMING INDEPENDENT PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to develop essential life skills for independence may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed independent life skills help teenagers and university freshmen manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders. At the same time, these practices build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents and foster stronger cooperation at school and in daily life.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in independent life skills has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**self-motivated**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. Teenagers and university freshmen can start with simple steps at school and in daily life, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**routine**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of teenagers and university freshmen valued independent life skills, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life, teenagers were twice as likely to manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When teenagers and university freshmen work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of teenagers and university freshmen valued independent life skills, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life, teenagers were twice as likely to manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When teenagers and university freshmen work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
When people first decide to focus on developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced independent life skills are far more effective when built step by step, helping teenagers and university freshmen manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how independent life skills can manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising independent life skills independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 8: Becoming Independent to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When teenagers and university freshmen see their close friends willingly engage in independent life skills, they are far more likely to join in and manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Why do many high school students agree that developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living is important, yet still find it difficult to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, teenagers and university freshmen can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on independent life skills. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 8: Becoming Independent report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, independent life skills stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**COMBINING TRADITIONAL VALUES WITH MODERN TOOLS IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living. Yet recent educational projects show that when used wisely, digital tools can actually strengthen independent life skills. Shared mobile calendars, reminder apps and online group checklists make it easier than ever for teenagers and university freshmen to manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders.
Of course, technology alone cannot solve every problem. Researchers warn against relying passively on apps while ignoring face-to-face communication, as <u>**they**</u> are only tools in the hands of users. <u>**Digital tools should serve as a practical bridge to support daily cooperation rather than a replacement for genuine human interaction.**</u>
When families and classmates combine smart reminders with warm personal encouragement, they can <u>**preserve**</u> the core spirit of Unit 8: Becoming Independent. For example, a quick evening message can remind everyone to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life before gathering for a friendly conversation.
Ultimately, blending modern convenience with timeless values helps communities <u>**enhance**</u> their daily routines and build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents in a sustainable way.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living. Rather than treating Unit 8: Becoming Independent as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on independent life skills. Through these authentic tasks, teenagers and university freshmen discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 8: BECOMING INDEPENDENT**
Practising independent life skills is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying developing time-management, budgeting and self-study skills for independent living have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to manage time, pocket money and household chores without reminders.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to develop essential life skills for independence at school and in daily life this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps teenagers and university freshmen build self-motivation, confidence and the trust of parents with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Becoming Independent)
